_comment: Missions campaign (docs/missions-design.md). One site, cargo first, then the crew. payload_kg is that mission's delivery; the cargo budget is every payload so far. checks: landing_safe, landing_clear, always_powered, water_per_sol (min L/sol), no_zone (kind). rover/lander: whether the scout rover and the crew lander are on site. player: robot (construction robot, Missions 2-3) or crew.

missions.title: Landing Zones
missions.situation: Your site is chosen and the landers are on their way. Every cargo lander, and later the crew, will come down inside a landing ellipse. Choose a safe landing zone, and where the base will go, far enough away that engine blast can't damage it.

requirements.text: The whole landing ellipse is on flat, safe ground
The base site is at least 12 m from the edge of the landing ellipse

stretch.text: Base within 40 m of the landing target: handy, but still safe

missions.title: Cargo Landing 1: Power and Water
missions.situation: The first cargo lander has touched down. Its construction robot (you) and GAR-Y, a small survey rover, must set up the power system and the ice drills before anyone leaves Earth. Nobody will be here to fix it: it has to run on its own, through every night and a dust storm.
missions.previous_line: Landing zone and base site chosen
missions.brief: You're the construction robot inside Cargo Lander 1. The crew won't leave Earth until their power and water are already working here.
missions.goal: Build a power system and ice drills that keep running, unattended, for 5 sols, through every night and a dust storm.

steps.how: Move the mouse to look. W A S D moves; hold Shift to go faster.

steps.text: Roll out of the cargo lander
steps.how: Look at the ramp door and press E to lower it, then drive down.
Press B outside. The site plan is a top-down view for placing rooms and equipment.
In the site plan, open Resources and place Solar Arrays on flat open ground. Power is cabled, so anywhere outside the landing zone works.
Rooms tab: drag out a Power & Engineering room. It's where the batteries live.

steps.text: Add an airlock to the room
steps.how: Structure tab: place an Airlock against the room's wall, outer end facing Mars. It's how the robot gets in.

steps.text: Add a battery bank inside it
steps.how: Go in through the airlock, then press B inside the room to furnish it. Batteries carry the drills through the night.

Orbital radar only shows where ice is likely. Hold G near GAR-Y and choose Find ice: it surveys the likely zone on its own, flags ice of 25% or more, and reports the best spot. (Survey there checks one spot you aim at.)

steps.text: Place an ice extractor where GAR-Y found ice
steps.how: Follow BEST ICE FOUND on your compass (it says LIKELY ICE until GAR-Y has found some). While placing, GAR-Y's measurements show on the ground: blue discs are ice, brown ones are dry. Richer ice makes more water.
Press T. It fast-forwards 5 sols, nights and the storm included, and shows what failed and why.

steps.text: Pass the test and complete the mission
steps.how: Not passing yet? Read the report, change one thing, and test again.

requirements.text: Power never runs out, through every night and the dust storm
The ice drills make at least 60 L of water a sol, ready for the crew

stretch.text: No reactor: solar and batteries only

hints: Press B to open the site plan. Power is under Resources.
A Power & Engineering room holds the batteries. Give it an airlock, walk in and press B to furnish it.
Solar arrays only work by day. Batteries carry the drills through the night.
Pale blue ground has the most ice. Hold G near GAR-Y and choose Survey there: it flags rich ice for your drills.
Press T to test your design: it fast-forwards 5 sols, including the storm.

missions.title: Cargo Landing 2: The Habitat
missions.nasa_step: Checking out the habitat before the crew launch
missions.situation: The second cargo lander has brought the habitat itself: rooms, an airlock and Life Support. Robots must build it and prove it works before the crew launch. Nobody is aboard yet, so the habitat has to keep itself warm and breathable on its own, powered by the system you built in Mission 2.
missions.brief: You're the construction robot inside Cargo Lander 2. It carries the habitat: rooms, an airlock and the Life Support machines.
missions.goal: Build a habitat that stays above 15 °C with breathable air for 10 sols, with nobody aboard, on your Mission 2 power system.

steps.how: Look at the ramp door and press E to lower it, then drive down.
Site plan, Rooms tab: drag out Life Support next to your Power & Engineering room, so they share a wall.
Walk into Life Support and press B. The thermal control unit keeps every room warm.
It splits water into oxygen and hydrogen. It needs power and water, so it depends on Mission 2.
It scrubs carbon dioxide from the air. Nobody is breathing yet, but the crew will be.
Where the crew will sleep. It has to stay warm too, so join it to the habitat.
Press T. It fast-forwards 10 sols and checks every room's temperature and the air.

steps.text: Pass the test and complete the mission
steps.how: Cold rooms? More heating, fewer windows, or less outside wall. Read the report and change one thing.

requirements.text: Every room stays above 15 °C for 10 sols
The air stays breathable: enough oxygen, little carbon dioxide
Power never runs out

stretch.text: Keep 15% of this mission's payload to spare

hints: Life Support holds the machines that keep everyone alive. Put it next to Power & Engineering.
Rooms lose heat through their outside walls and windows. Compact bases stay warmer.
The thermal control unit heats every connected room. A wall heater can top up a cold one.
Press T to test: 10 sols, every night included.

missions.title: The Crew Land
missions.situation: The habitat passed its checks, so the crew launched. Months later, their lander touches down inside your landing ellipse. Four people now depend on everything you built. Make the habitat a place they can live: beds, food, water and hygiene.
missions.brief: You're one of four crew inside the lander. Outside is the base your robots built.
missions.goal: Keep four crew safe for their first 10 sols: oxygen, carbon dioxide, water, food and temperature all in the safe range.

steps.text: Open the hatch and step onto Mars
steps.how: Look at the hatch and press E. Walk down the ramp.
Follow BASE SITE on your compass. Press E at the airlock door.
In Living Quarters, press B. Every crew member needs a berth.
Build a Galley and add the kitchenette: its rehydration tap brings freeze-dried food back to life.
Build a Hygiene room. The water reclaimer recycles about 93% of the crew's water.
Press T. It fast-forwards 10 sols with four people breathing, eating and drinking.

steps.text: Pass the test and complete the mission
steps.how: The report says what went wrong first. Fix that, then test again.

requirements.text: There are bunks for all four crew
Oxygen, carbon dioxide, water, food and temperature stay safe for 10 sols

stretch.text: No water reclaimer: bring enough water instead

hints: Four people breathe out about 4 kg of carbon dioxide a sol. The air recycler removes it.
Each person drinks and washes with about 10 L of water a sol. Reclaiming it saves the drills.
The crew lander brought 60 sols of food. Growing more comes in Mission 6.
Press T to test. You can walk around the base too: it's yours now.

missions.title: Dust Storm Season
missions.situation: Dust storm season has arrived, and this one is planet-wide, like the 2018 storm that ended the Opportunity rover's mission. Mission Control forecasts seven sols of dust so thick it blocks nine-tenths of the sunlight: the solar arrays will make almost nothing. Life support must stay on the whole time, even if other things have to switch off.
missions.brief: A seven-sol, planet-wide dust storm is coming. Solar power will drop to a tenth.
missions.goal: Keep life support powered and the habitat warm all the way through the storm, and keep the crew's health above 80%. This landing brings one compact nuclear reactor: it helps, but in a big storm the dust filters and frozen outside kit need extra power, so it can't carry the base on its own.

steps.how: It arrived on this landing. Site plan, Power tab: 8 kW day and night, storm or not, like NASA's Kilopower. In the storm the base needs more than that, so it can't do it alone: you'll need batteries charged before the storm too.
Press T. It runs 11 sols, with a 7-sol storm from sol 2 that blocks 90% of the sunlight. Watch the battery line on the graph.

steps.text: Pass the test and complete the mission
steps.how: Heating is the big load, and it switches off before life support. Ran out? Add battery banks and charge them before the storm, add solar arrays (even 10% of the sun adds up), and turn lights off in empty rooms.

requirements.text: Life support has power through the whole storm
The habitat stays above 15 °C
Crew health stays above 80%

stretch.text: No power cuts at all, even lights and labs

hints: In a storm, power is shared by priority: life support first, then heating, lights, and last labs and drills.
A big storm adds work: fine dust clogs the air filters and outside kit needs heating, so life support uses about 3 kW more until it ends.
Work out what life support needs: the power used line during the storm, times five sols. That's how much stored or steady power you need.
A reactor runs day and night, storm or not. It's heavy, but you have this landing's payload.
Batteries only help if there's spare power to charge them before the storm. Dimming empty rooms saves power too.
Press T to test: the storm starts on sol 2.

missions.title: Toward Self-Sufficiency
missions.situation: Two more crew are on their way, with a supply lander carrying 60 sols of food for everyone. After that, the next resupply is a long way off. To last, the base must start growing its own food and doing the science the crew came for. This is the final test: six crew, 100 sols.
missions.brief: Six crew, 100 sols, and the next resupply is a long way off.
missions.goal: Keep six crew safe for 100 sols while growing at least a quarter of their food and running research.

steps.how: Two more people are coming. Add bunks in Living Quarters.
Plants need light, water and warmth. Join it to the habitat.

steps.text: Grow at least a quarter of the crew's food
steps.how: Anything that grows food counts: grow trays, seedling stations, planters. Each grow tray feeds about 4% of six people. They use power and water too.

steps.text: Build a Science Lab with a workbench
steps.how: Research is why the crew came. A workbench lets them start.
Press T. It fast-forwards 100 sols: about three months on Mars.

steps.text: Pass the test and complete the mission
steps.how: Food running out? Grow more, or add storage. Check power and water first: plants need both.

requirements.text: There are bunks for all six crew
The base grows at least 25% of the crew's food
The crew are doing research
Oxygen, carbon dioxide, water, food and temperature stay safe for 100 sols

stretch.text: Send GAR-Y for a core sample for the Science Lab (+20% research)

hints: Six people eat about 11 kg of food a sol. Each grow tray grows about 0.4 kg.
Six people need more oxygen and more CO₂ scrubbing than four: check the oxygen generators and air recyclers.
Grow lights use a lot of power. Check the night and the storms still work.
Plants drink water. Your ice drills and reclaimer have to keep up.
Press T to test all 100 sols.
Toward self-sufficiency: a regolith printer (Storage) fed by a regolith intake outside makes Mars-made material for walls, shelves and crates, so your cargo stretches further.

missions.title: Solar Storm Shelter
missions.previous_line: The base grows food and does research
missions.situation: Act 2: living on Mars. Mars has no global magnetic field and a thin atmosphere, so radiation from the Sun reaches the ground. Orbiters watching the Sun can warn of a solar particle event (a burst of high-energy protons from a solar flare) only about half an hour before it arrives. The crew need a shielded room to shelter in for a day.
missions.brief: A solar flare is coming. The crew need a shielded shelter, and only half an hour to get there.
missions.goal: Build a storm shelter that keeps the crew's radiation dose under 50 mSv through a solar particle event, while the rest of the base keeps running.

steps.text: Make a storm shelter: place a Storm Shelter Locker
steps.how: Interior build (Shift+B), in any room with space for everyone: that room becomes the storm shelter, where the crew wait out a solar particle event.

The hull gives 5 points. Shield the shelter room itself: Site plan, Structure tab, or from inside (Shift+B, aim at a wall or the ceiling). Roof shielding over the whole room adds 12, and each regolith wall panel (printed from Mars soil, 8) or water wall (10) adds its points × 1.5 shared over the room's floor squares, like shield blocks and water wall panels inside it. A small shelter is quicker to protect.
Press T. A solar particle event arrives on sol 4. The crew go to the shelter and stay a day.

steps.text: Pass the test and complete the mission
steps.how: Too much radiation? Add more shielding panels to the outside. The shelter needs a floor square for every 3 crew.

requirements.text: The shelter has 20+ shield points, room for everyone, and heating
The crew's dose in the event stays under 50 mSv
Air, water, food and temperature stay safe

stretch.text: Bunks for everyone inside the shelter, so the crew sleep shielded every night

hints: Shelter shield points = 5 (the hull) + 1.5 × the shelter room's shielding (its roof, its outside walls, blocks and water walls inside) ÷ its floor squares.

Roof shielding over the whole shelter adds 12: most radiation comes from overhead. Regolith wall panels add 8 each (printed from Mars soil, so no cargo from Earth once you're printing), a water wall 10.
A window can't be shielded: choose a shelter room without windows, or shield its other walls.
Lockers, pantry cabinets and sample cabinets in the shelter add a little more there.
The shelter must be warm: the crew stay there a whole day. Check it isn't a cold spot.
Wayfinding panels point the way to the shelter during an event.

missions.title: The Long Day's Work
missions.nasa_step: Living on Mars: gravity and the crew
missions.previous_line: The crew have a radiation shelter
missions.situation: Six people, 30 sols, real work. In Mars gravity (38% of Earth's) bones and muscles weaken unless the crew exercise. Living in a small base far from home is hard on everyone too. And on sol 12, the Engineer is hurt in an accident. Earth is up to 24 minutes away by message, so the Doctor treats them here.
missions.brief: The crew become people: names, jobs, fitness and wellbeing. Someone will get hurt.
missions.goal: Keep all six crew fit and well for 30 sols, care for the injured Engineer, and keep the science and the food going.

steps.how: Open Mission Control (M) and choose Crew. Give your six crew their names.
Each powered exercise station keeps about 3 crew fit. Six crew need two.

steps.text: A Medical Bay with an exam cot
steps.how: Build a Medical Bay (if you haven't) and place an exam cot.
Medicines and trauma kits, in the Medical Bay.
Build a Mission Operations room and put a communications station inside it, then place the Communications Mast outside (site plan, Surface gear tab). Together they're the crew's contact with Earth.
The Crew screen (Mission Control, Crew) lists six needs: sleep, space, meals together, a bit of home, meaningful work and contact with Earth. Meet at least four. Each one says what it's missing.
Press T. It runs 30 sols. The Engineer is injured on sol 12.

steps.text: Pass the test and complete the mission
steps.how: Check the Crew screen: it says what each need is missing.

requirements.text: Everyone's fitness stays above 70%
Average wellbeing stays above 60%
The injured Engineer recovers by sol 22
The crew keep up at least 1 research a sol
Air, water, food and temperature stay safe

hints: Fitness falls a little every sol in Mars gravity. Powered exercise stations bring it back up.
Each person has a favourite thing (it's on the Crew screen). Having it in the base cheers them up.
Noise matters: bunks next to Power & Engineering or Life Support sleep badly.
Everyone has a job, and a room to do it in. Someone without their work room loses heart.
Injured crew can't work. The others cover, so work slows down until they recover.

missions.title: Hull Breach
missions.nasa_step: Living on Mars: a hostile, closed environment
missions.previous_line: The crew are fit and well
missions.situation: A micrometeoroid (a grain of space rock moving faster than a bullet) punches a hole in the hull. Air starts rushing out. How bad it gets depends on your floor plan: hatches seal automatically, but open connections don't. Real stations are built in sections that can be sealed off for exactly this reason.
missions.brief: A hole in the hull. Your floor plan decides how much air you lose.
missions.goal: Keep the habitat's air pressure above 70% through a hull breach, patch the hole within 2 hours, and have full pressure back within 6.

steps.how: Emergency patches and sealant. The Engineer can patch a hole in an hour with it.

Stored air (mostly nitrogen) to refill a section once the hole is patched. Not the Oxygen Reserve, which is breathing oxygen for when the oxygen generator fails. It goes in Life Support, Storage, Engineering, an airlock or a corridor, and works for the whole base wherever it is. Each rack refills about 2 floor squares.
Rooms joined without a hatch share their air. Put interior doors (hatches) at corridor ends so no section is more than 40% of the base.
Press T. A breach hits Living Quarters on sol 3 at 02:00. The Test runs 4 sols.

steps.text: Pass the test and complete the mission
steps.how: Air pressure too low? Make the breached section smaller with hatches. Not refilled? Add air reserve racks.

requirements.text: Air pressure stays above 70%
The hole is patched within 2 hours
Full pressure is back within 6 hours
Air, water, food and temperature stay safe

stretch.text: Survive a breach in any room: the Test tries each one

hints: Air pressure is the share of the habitat that still holds its air.
A corridor end with no hatch joins rooms into one big section. Add an interior door there.
A bigger section vents more slowly, but loses more air in the end.
Each air reserve rack holds enough air to refill about 2 floor squares.

missions.title: The Long Silence
missions.nasa_step: Living on Mars: isolation and distance
missions.previous_line: The base survived a hull breach
missions.situation: The finale. For 200 sols the crew are on their own, and Mars passes behind the Sun: for 14 sols there's no contact with Earth at all. Machines break, someone gets hurt, the Sun flares and a dust storm rolls in. You can't predict exactly when. So the Test runs three different futures, and your base has to survive all of them.
missions.brief: 200 sols, things break, and for 14 of them Earth can't hear you.
missions.goal: Keep six crew safe, fit and well for 200 sols, in three different futures, with breakdowns, an injury, a solar particle event, a dust storm and a communications blackout.

steps.how: Interior build (Shift+B): a Spare Parts Rack (Storage, Engineering, Life Support or a corridor) holds eight parts. The Engineer uses one for each repair, and a running regolith printer makes more.
Air recycler, oxygen generator, water reclaimer and thermal control unit: if one breaks, the second keeps the crew alive while it's repaired.
The next resupply is 100 sols away. Grow trays, planters and seedling stations all count. The step shows how much you grow now.
Press T. It runs 200 sols three times (three futures), each with different breakdowns and events. It takes a little while.

steps.text: Pass all three and complete the campaign
steps.how: Read which future failed and why. A robust base survives bad luck, not just one test.

requirements.text: Air, water, food and temperature stay safe for 200 sols
No life-critical system is down for more than 12 hours
Everyone's fitness stays above 70%
Average wellbeing stays above 60%, even in the blackout
The solar particle event dose stays under 50 mSv
The base grows at least half the food
The crew keep up at least 1 research a sol

stretch.text: No system down for more than 2 hours

hints: Redundancy: two of everything life-critical. When one breaks, the other carries on.
Each repair uses a spare part. No spares, no repair. Eight machines break about eight times in 200 sols: one rack is cutting it fine. A running regolith printer makes more.
The blackout takes away contact with Earth, so wellbeing drops. Meet the other needs well before it starts.
The three futures are different, but the same every time you test, so you can compare versions fairly.
